conventions.convention: A DFA over an alphabet \(\Sigma\) includes \(\Sigma\) in its data, and its transition function \(\delta\) is total on \(Q\times\Sigma\).
Words over \(\Sigma\) are finite sequences, \(\varepsilon\) is the unique length-\(0\) word, concatenation is defined on such words, and \(\Sigma^*\) is the set of all finite words over \(\Sigma\).
Boolean operations on languages are taken inside one fixed ambient \(\Sigma^*\); in particular, complement means \(\Sigma^*\setminus L\).

The prefix-state set \(S_B\) consists of the \(B\)-avoiding proper prefixes of words in \(B\); when \(B\) is finite, nonempty, and consists of nonempty words, \(\varepsilon\in S_B\) and \(S_B\) is finite.
A parse tree is finite, rooted, ordered by finite-sequence addresses, and a variable leaf witnessing an \(\varepsilon\)-production contributes no terminal symbol to the yield.
A leftmost derivation rewrites the leftmost remaining variable at each step, and a rightmost derivation rewrites the rightmost remaining variable at each step.
Chomsky normal form permits an \(\varepsilon\)-production only as the special start-symbol rule \(S\to\varepsilon\), with \(S\) absent from every right-hand side.
In the substitution lemma, the displayed productions \(B\to w_1,\ldots,B\to w_m\) are exactly the full family of \(B\)-productions in \(G\).

load_bearing.statement: A **context-free grammar** is a quadruple $$ G=(V,\Sigma,P,S) $$ such that: - \(V\) is a finite set of **variables**. - \(\Sigma\) is a finite alphabet of **terminals**, disjoint from \(V\). - \(S\in V\) is the **start variable**. - \(P\) is a finite set of **productions** of the form \(A\to\alpha\), where \(A\in V\) and \(\alpha\) is a finite word over the alphabet \(V\cup\Sigma\).

A deterministic finite automaton over \(\Sigma\) is a quintuple \(D=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,q_0,F)\) with finite state set \(Q\), start state \(q_0\in Q\), accepting set \(F\subseteq Q\), and total transition function \(\delta:Q\times\Sigma\to Q\).

Let \(G=(V,\Sigma,P,S)\) be a context-free grammar. The **language generated by \(G\)** is $$ L(G):=\{w\in\Sigma^*: S\Rightarrow_G^* w\}. $$ A language \(L\) over \(\Sigma\) is **context-free** when \(L=L(G)\) for some context-free grammar \(G\) over \(\Sigma\).
A word \(w\in\Sigma^*\) is **accepted by \(D\)** when $$ \delta^*(q_0,w)\in F. $$ The **language recognized by \(D\)** is $$ L(D):=\{w\in\Sigma^*: \delta^*(q_0,w)\in F\}. $$

Write \(\beta\Rightarrow_G\gamma\) when there exist words \(x,y\), a variable \(A\in V\), and a production \(A\to\alpha\) in \(P\) such that \(\beta=xAy\) and \(\gamma=x\alpha y\). Write \(\beta\Rightarrow_G^*\gamma\) when \(\gamma\) is obtained from \(\beta\) by finitely many one-step derivations, possibly zero.

For every context-free grammar \(G\) there exists a context-free grammar \(G_\varepsilon\) such that: 1. \(G_\varepsilon\) has no \(\varepsilon\)-productions and \(L(G_\varepsilon)=L(G)\setminus\{\varepsilon\}.\) 2. If \(\varepsilon\in L(G)\), then there exists a context-free grammar \(G'\) with \(L(G')=L(G)\) whose only \(\varepsilon\)-production is a start-symbol rule \(S_0\to\varepsilon\), where \(S_0\) does not occur on any right-hand side.
Every context-free grammar has an equivalent context-free grammar in Chomsky normal form.

Let \(G\) be a context-free grammar containing the production \(A\to uBv\). Suppose the productions of \(B\) in \(G\) are exactly \(B\to w_1,\ldots,B\to w_m\). Let \(H\) be the grammar obtained by deleting \(A\to uBv\) and replacing it by \(A\to uw_1v,\ldots,A\to uw_mv\), while keeping every other production of \(G\). Then \(L(H)=L(G)\).

Let \(G=(V,\Sigma,P,S)\) be a context-free grammar and let \(w\in\Sigma^*\). 1. The word \(w\) is derived from \(S\) in \(G\) if and only if there exists a parse tree for \(G\) with yield \(w\). 2. Every parse tree for \(G\) determines a unique leftmost derivation of its yield and a unique rightmost derivation of its yield.

Let \(D=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,q_0,F)\) be a DFA. An **extended transition function** for \(D\) is a function \(\delta^*:Q\times\Sigma^*\to Q\) satisfying \(\delta^*(q,\varepsilon)=q\) for every \(q\in Q\), and \(\delta^*(q,ua)=\delta(\delta^*(q,u),a)\) for every state \(q\in Q\), every word \(u\in\Sigma^*\), and every letter \(a\in\Sigma\).

For every DFA \(D=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,q_0,F)\) there exists a unique function \(\delta^*:Q\times\Sigma^*\to Q\) such that, for all \(q\in Q\), \(u\in\Sigma^*\), and \(a\in\Sigma\), \(\delta^*(q,\varepsilon)=q\) and \(\delta^*(q,ua)=\delta(\delta^*(q,u),a)\).

published_dependencies.used_for: Provides the alphabet, word, empty-word, concatenation, and \(\Sigma^*\) conventions used throughout the DFA and CFG pages.
Supplies the total-function convention behind DFA transition maps and alphabet maps.
Supplies finiteness for DFA state sets, CFG data, and the finite prefix-state constructions.
Types the DFA transition function as a map on \(Q\times\Sigma\).
Types recognized and generated languages as subsets of a fixed \(\Sigma^*\).
Fixes union, intersection, difference, and complement for regular-language closure arguments.
Defines forbidden-factor avoidance and the proper-prefix state set \(S_B\) used in the sink-state DFA extension.
Provides the published longest-suffix prefix automaton extended in the factor-avoidance proposition.
Types one-step derivation as a relation on sentential forms.
Provides the rooted ordered tree model used to define parse trees.
Provides the induced word map \(\widehat h\) used in CFL closure under homomorphism.

concerns.concern: Proof step 2.1 only sketches the compression/expansion between derivations in \(G\) and \(G_\varepsilon\) via ‘maximal families of nullable subderivations’; the standard correspondence is believable, but the proof leaves the formal induction on derivation trees to the reader.

Proof steps 2.1 and 2.2 describe compressing and re-expanding maximal unit-production blocks at a high level; preservation of the special start-symbol \(\varepsilon\)-case inherited from [L1] is implicit rather than shown explicitly.

Proof steps 2.1 and 3.1 give the downward cleanup of original and auxiliary variables only schematically; termination of the repeated substitutions is inferable from the variable ordering set up in step 1.1, but that well-foundedness argument is not written out.
